scripts.comment: A custom block is a set of predefined instructions designed to perform a specific task. They help you simplify your code within your project. Custom blocks can also accept multiple input parameters, allowing them to adapt dynamically to different needs. Playing with arcs are fun. In this session, a custom block called 'Petal' is made. The block generates one petal with a specified radius and degrees. The value that is entered in the white area is passed to your code in the custom block. Vary the radius and degrees to see the different petals that are generated.

In this code, the 'Petal' block is rotated around its origin. A variable 'n' was made for the number of flower petals. A full circle is 360 degrees. If you want to place 'n' petals evenly around the circle, each petal must be rotated 360/n. This routine then creates a flower of n-petals.

Using the previous code, a flower with a stem and leaves can be made. After making the flower, the turtle is moved with the 'point in direction' block. This 'point in direction' block orients the turtle in the direction that you want to go to make the stem. A stem was created with two arc blocks. The 'point in direction' block is used again to orient the turtle in the correct direction to make two leaves. The leaves are created with two 'petal' blocks that are aligned with the 'point in direction' block. Please note, a 'turn' block could have been used in this code instead of the 'point in direction' block. Both commands require you to move the turtle and test the correct placement.

Try out the 'point in direction' block using the dropdown menu. The turtle will move as follows: 0° = Pointing up (north) 90° = Pointing right (east) 180° = Pointing down (south) 270° = Pointing left (west) Custom degrees can be used by typing in a number in the white space or clicking on the down arrow and moving the arrow dial.

In this code, I will make another flower. I make a custom block named "flower". I use all of the code from before except the reset, set 'n' and the embroidery stitch. This will allow me to change parameters without having to recode the block. Try it out. I made a flower with six petals here.

I want to make multiple flowers. I can do it a couple of ways. I need to use a "pen up" block to move the turtle without leaving a trail. I need to orient the turtle in the correct direction and then move it. The "pen down" will start the turtle to leave a trail. I made two flowers with different number of petals. In the variable palette, there is a box to check and uncheck next to the defined variable 'n'. When the box is checked, the value of 'n' is shown on the stage area.

I want the flowers to be in a specific location. I will use the "go to x, y" block. Again I must use the "pen up" and "pen down" block to move the turtle without leaving a trail. Since the first flower's center was at the origin, (0,0). I know that the x coordinate is 0. I want to move the turtle to the right to make another flower that is parallel to the first. Try out different 'x' values to see where the turtle goes. If your turtle is not showing. Click on the turtle in the ribbon at the top of this window. In the drop down menu, uncllick "hide turtle".

In this code, I add another flower, this time, I put the third flower in another location on the other side of the original one. Notice that there are two jumps after the program is run. This is shown below the stage area. Click on the turtle in the ribbon at the top of this window. In the drop down menu, uncllick "hide jump" stitches to see where they will be placed. The x in the jump stitches is not efficient because it goes over the previous design. A better way would have been to continue to move the turtle right.
The turtle is moved to the right after each flower is made. Notice the red jump stitches.
